title: Rethinking Representations for World-Action Modeling

paper.title: Rethinking Representations for World-Action Modeling
paper.abstract: Abstract World-action models jointly learn robot policies and predict future observations, making the representation space an interface between control and prediction. We study the design of this space through controlled comparisons, finding that neither reconstruction fidelity nor pre-trained perceptual features alone ensure effective policy learning. These findings motivate ReWAM, a representation-centric world-action model built on pre-trained DINO features. Feature Calibration and a Temporal Representation Bottleneck organize these features into compact world states suited to dynamics modeling. Action-Grounded Representation Shaping routes only action-loss gradients to the bottleneck, thereby letting the policy shape what the representation encodes while the world model learns how it evolves. Without generative video pre-training, ReWAM achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0. On RoboDojo, it achieves an average score of 12.29 and a success rate of 8.28% using approximately 600 hours of embodied pre-training data.

sections.heading: \calmregular Introduction
sections.text: World-action models (WAMs) jointly learn robot policies and predict how the world evolves. Many recent WAMs ( Bi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Ye et al., 2026c ; Yuan et al., 2026b ) build on pre-trained video generators and predict future observations in the latent space of a video variational autoencoder (Video-VAE). These models inherit dynamics priors from large-scale generative video pre-training, but their latent spaces are typically optimized for visual reconstruction. Such spaces may preserve fine-grained appearance details without explicitly prioritizing information relevant to control. The role of world prediction extends beyond producing explicit visual rollouts. Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) retains video co-training while removing future-video denoising at deployment, suggesting that prediction can benefit policies through joint training. This raises a fundamental question: How should the representation space for world-action modeling be defined? Representation-space WAMs use pre-trained perceptual features or learned visual-action tokenizers ( Lyu et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Comparative studies show that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to assess control utility ( Nilaksh et al., 2026 ; Yeom et al., 2026 ) . Our experiments support this distinction: without generative video pre-training, raw DINO features outperform Video-VAE latents on RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , despite lower pixel-reconstruction SSIM. Reconstruction-oriented latents therefore do not by themselves establish effective representations for policy learning. Perceptual features are also not necessarily well suited to dynamics modeling: frame-wise features do not explicitly encode temporal variation, and their statistics may be poorly matched to diffusion training. Calibrating DINO features through multi-layer aggregation, normalization, and a representation-aware diffusion noise schedule improves average success on RoboTwin 2.0 by 12.20 12.20 percentage points. Representation design thus extends beyond the choice of encoder. It must also address how features are prepared for prediction, organized over time, and adapted to the needs of control. We propose a division of roles: the policy shapes what the representation encodes, while the world model learns how that representation evolves. We introduce ReWAM , a representation-centric WAM that implements this principle through Action-Grounded Representation Shaping (AGRS). Feature Calibration prepares frozen DINO features for diffusion modeling, and a Temporal Representation Bottleneck (TRB) organizes them into compact world states. During joint training, AGRS routes only action-loss gradients to the bottleneck, adapting the representation to action prediction. The world model learns how this representation evolves without updating it through its own prediction loss. Fig. 1 provides an overview of ReWAM. Figure 1 : Overview of representations for world-action modeling. Top-left: Video-VAE latents are optimized for visual reconstruction. Top-right: Frozen DINO features inherit priors from perceptual pre-training. Bottom: ReWAM uses a Temporal Representation Bottleneck (TRB) to form compact world states from calibrated DINO features. Action-Grounded Representation Shaping (AGRS) trains the TRB through asymmetric routing of action-loss gradients, while the world model learns state transitions. Without generative video pre-training, ReWAM achieves 93.6% success in both the clean and random settings of RoboTwin 2.0 and leads the compared methods without embodied pre-training on RoboDojo ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . Embodied pre-training further improves its RoboDojo average score to 12.29 and success rate to 8.28%. Together with real-robot evaluations, these findings highlight a promising path for world-action modeling based on pre-trained perceptual priors and representations shaped by the demands of control, without relying on generative video pre-training. Our contributions are threefold: • We show through controlled comparisons that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient for choosing WAM representations, and that perceptual features benefit from calibration for dynamics modeling. • We introduce ReWAM, which lets the action objective shape a compact representation space for joint prediction and control. • We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design without generative video pre-training across two simulation benchmarks and real-robot tasks.

sections.heading: \calmregular World-Action Models
sections.text: Unified video and action models couple dynamics prediction with policy learning ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ) . Recent systems build on video generation through joint denoising ( Ye et al., 2026c ) or interactions between world and action streams ( Bi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Motubrain Team et al., 2026 ) . RxBrain ( Liang et al., 2026 ) and Cosmos 3 ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) extend this framework to broader multimodal understanding and generation. Other approaches expose intermediate generative features to the policy ( Pai et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) . Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) removes future-video denoising at deployment, while Faster-WAM ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) studies sparse interactions between video and action prediction under distribution shift. These studies motivate examining how the shared representation interface supports policy learning. Complementary work enriches visual prediction with geometric, motion, and semantic supervision ( Guo et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026c ; Yuan et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026a ) , or aligns policy features with future visual representations ( Zheng et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) . Representation-space approaches use pre-trained visual features for prediction and control. LDA-1B ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) and DexWorldModel ( Deng et al., 2026 ) directly predict DINO features, while VLA-JEPA ( Sun et al., 2026 ) and Being-H0.7 ( Luo et al., 2026 ) use future observations to supervise latent representations that guide action generation. LaWAM ( Chen et al., 2026a ) predicts latent visual subgoals, and GAM ( Han et al., 2026 ) uses geometric foundation features for prediction and action decoding. Learned visual-action tokenizers adapt the interface between perception and control ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , while residual latent actions model changes in DINO features ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) . ReWAM builds on this line of work by calibrating and temporally organizing pre-trained features, then using asymmetric gradient routing to adapt the prediction space to the policy objective during joint world-action training.

sections.heading: \calmregular Representations for Prediction and Generation
sections.text: Predictive learning in visual feature spaces supports representation learning and world modeling, as explored by V-JEPA models ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) , DINO-world ( Baldassarre et al., 2025 ) , and Spa3R ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Representation design also matters for generation. REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ) and VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) align denoiser features and autoencoder latents, respectively, with pre-trained representations. The representation autoencoder (RAE) ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) uses pre-trained encoders to define generative latent spaces, with subsequent work extending this approach to video generation ( Xie et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026b ) and interactive world modeling ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Probing studies and comparative analyses examine what representations encode and how they support spatial understanding, dynamics prediction, and control ( Huang et al., 2026b ; Yeom et al., 2026 ; Nilaksh et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026a ) . ReWAM addresses the complementary problem of how to construct and adapt a representation space for joint world prediction and policy learning.

\calmregular Experiments \calmregular Setup Implementation Details. ReWAM uses frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) features and UMT5 embeddings of language instructions. The world and action DiT branches each contain 30 layers, with hidden widths of 2048 2048 and 1024 1024 , respectively, and approximately 3.58B parameters in total. Head-camera images are resized to 256 × 320 256	imes 320 pixels and wrist-camera images to 128 × 160 128	imes 160 pixels. Actions and proprioception are represented as 14-dimensional joint-and-gripper vectors and standardized using z-score normalization. We train with AdamW on 32 H20 GPUs, with a batch size of 512 and a peak learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} that decays to 10 − 6 10^{-6} on a cosine schedule. RoboTwin 2.0. We train a multi-task policy on the 50-task RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark ( Chen et al., 2025 ) using 2,500 clean trajectories and 25,000 trajectories from the random setting. The main comparison uses five training epochs, aligned with the baseline protocol. Representation comparisons and ablations, including the Fast-WAM baselines, use a matched one-epoch training budget. We evaluate 100 episodes per task in each of the clean and random settings and average success rates across tasks. RoboDojo. We evaluate on the simulation suite of RoboDojo ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , which covers five capability categories: Generalization, Precision, Long-Horizon, Memory, and Open. The training set contains 3,500 trajectories across 35 tasks. We train ReWAM for 50k steps with and without prior embodied pre-training. We report the benchmark’s partial-progress score and binary success rate, averaging each metric across the five categories and comparing methods within each pre-training setting. Embodied Pre-training. To assess the benefit of embodied pre-training with additional data, we pre-train ReWAM and Fast-WAM for 75k steps on the same 600 hours of self-collected real-robot manipulation demonstrations. The dataset covers a broad range of manipulation tasks, with collection environments and camera settings that differ from those used in our downstream real-robot experiments. Real-Robot Evaluation. We evaluate ReWAM on a bimanual Piper platform across three tasks: Collect Objects, Fold Clothes, and Unpack Lunchbox. After embodied pre-training, ReWAM and Fast-WAM each undergo 10k steps of task-specific post-training on demonstrations collected in the target scene. We report success rates over 20 trials per task. \calmregular Main Results ReWAM achieves 93.6% success in both settings of RoboTwin 2.0 ( sec. 3.4 ), exceeding the strongest compared method by 0.2 0.2 percentage points on clean and 1.4 1.4 points on random. Its performance in the random setting indicates robustness to the benchmark’s scene variations without embodied pre-training. On RoboDojo, ReWAM leads the compared methods without embodied pre-training, with an average score of 9.42 9.42 and a success rate of 5.82 % 5.82\% ( sec. 3.4 ). Embodied pre-training raises these results to 12.29 12.29 and 8.28 % 8.28\% , highlighting ReWAM’s potential to improve further with larger-scale embodied training data. In this setting, ReWAM achieves the highest Generalization score and success rate and the highest Long-Horizon success rate. The benefits of embodied pre-training vary across capabilities. Generalization and Long-Horizon success rates rise from 4.33 % 4.33\% to 10.50 % 10.50\% and from 11.00 % 11.00\% to 16.25 % 16.25\% , respectively. (2025a) . ReWAM also falls substantially behind the leading methods in Open instruction following. We compare Video-VAE and DINO WAMs in tab. 6 . Removing generative video pre-training reduces Fast-WAM’s success by 21.68 / 24.11 21.68/24.11 percentage points on clean/random. Without this pre-training, raw DINO features outperform Video-VAE latents by 4.90 / 9.22 4.90/9.22 points, despite lower RGB reconstruction SSIM ( 0.70 0.70 versus 0.91 0.91 ). An RGB reconstruction codec likewise yields lower success than a DINO reconstruction codec ( tab. 6 ). Reconstruction fidelity thus does not necessarily ensure a representation’s utility for control. Feature Calibration. Progressively calibrating DINO features with normalization, a representation-aware noise schedule, and multi-layer aggregation yields successive gains of 3.92 3.92 , 1.41 1.41 , and 6.87 6.87 percentage points in average success, as detailed in tab. 6 . Together, these components improve average success by 12.20 12.20 points over raw DINO features. The gains indicate that pre-trained perceptual features benefit from calibration to the distribution and structure required by diffusion-based dynamics modeling. Temporal Representation Bottleneck. To assess temporal organization, we compare the representation designs in tab. 6 . Fixed random projection concatenates features at each spatial location across a temporal window and projects them to 512 512 dimensions. This simple construction improves average success by 2.89 2.89 percentage points over the calibrated frame-wise baseline, highlighting the value of temporal organization. The result is consistent with prior work on fixed random projections of pre-trained DINO features as prediction latents ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . We also pre-train the TRB as a codec to reconstruct RGB images or DINO features and freeze it during WAM training. The RGB reconstruction codec substantially reduces success, whereas the DINO reconstruction codec falls slightly below fixed random projection on average, suggesting that reconstruction-based training alone is insufficient to improve these temporal representations for control. Action-Grounded Representation Shaping. AGRS achieves 90.70 % / 89.12 % 90.70\%/89.12\% success on clean/random, outperforming fixed random projection by 3.94 / 3.18 3.94/3.18 percentage points in tab. 6 . The gradient-routing ablation in tab. 6 supports keeping world-loss gradients out of the TRB: allowing them through the current-representation path reduces average success by 6.30 6.30 percentage points, and allowing them through both current and future paths degrades performance further. These results suggest that letting the world objective reshape its prediction targets may encourage representation collapse or predictive shortcuts. The dimensionality comparison in tab. 6 highlights a further advantage of AGRS. Reducing fixed random projection from 512 512 to 128 128 dimensions lowers average success by 3.29 3.29 percentage points. AGRS performs best among the tested widths at 128 128 dimensions and remains effective at 64 64 dimensions. This contrast suggests that action grounding learns more effective control representations, enabling strong performance even at substantially lower dimensionality. Reconstruction fidelity alone does not determine control performance, and pre-trained perceptual features benefit from calibration and temporal organization. ReWAM combines these components with action-grounded representation shaping, letting the policy determine what the representation encodes, while the world model learns its dynamics. Results on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, and real-robot manipulation demonstrate the effectiveness of this design without generative video pre-training. sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: ReWAM uses frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) features and UMT5 embeddings of language instructions. The world and action DiT branches each contain 30 layers, with hidden widths of 2048 2048 and 1024 1024 , respectively, and approximately 3.58B parameters in total. Head-camera images are resized to 256 × 320 256\times 320 pixels and wrist-camera images to 128 × 160 128\times 160 pixels. Actions and proprioception are represented as 14-dimensional joint-and-gripper vectors and standardized using z-score normalization. We train with AdamW on 32 H20 GPUs, with a batch size of 512 and a peak learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} that decays to 10 − 6 10^{-6} on a cosine schedule.

sections.heading: RoboTwin 2.0.
sections.text: We train a multi-task policy on the 50-task RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark ( Chen et al., 2025 ) using 2,500 clean trajectories and 25,000 trajectories from the random setting. The main comparison uses five training epochs, aligned with the baseline protocol. Representation comparisons and ablations, including the Fast-WAM baselines, use a matched one-epoch training budget. We evaluate 100 episodes per task in each of the clean and random settings and average success rates across tasks.

sections.heading: RoboDojo.
sections.text: We evaluate on the simulation suite of RoboDojo ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , which covers five capability categories: Generalization, Precision, Long-Horizon, Memory, and Open. The training set contains 3,500 trajectories across 35 tasks. We train ReWAM for 50k steps with and without prior embodied pre-training. We report the benchmark’s partial-progress score and binary success rate, averaging each metric across the five categories and comparing methods within each pre-training setting.

sections.heading: Embodied Pre-training.
sections.text: To assess the benefit of embodied pre-training with additional data, we pre-train ReWAM and Fast-WAM for 75k steps on the same 600 hours of self-collected real-robot manipulation demonstrations. The dataset covers a broad range of manipulation tasks, with collection environments and camera settings that differ from those used in our downstream real-robot experiments.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate ReWAM on a bimanual Piper platform across three tasks: Collect Objects, Fold Clothes, and Unpack Lunchbox. After embodied pre-training, ReWAM and Fast-WAM each undergo 10k steps of task-specific post-training on demonstrations collected in the target scene. We report success rates over 20 trials per task.

sections.heading: \calmregular Main Results
sections.text: ReWAM achieves 93.6% success in both settings of RoboTwin 2.0 ( sec. 3.4 ), exceeding the strongest compared method by 0.2 0.2 percentage points on clean and 1.4 1.4 points on random. Its performance in the random setting indicates robustness to the benchmark’s scene variations without embodied pre-training. On RoboDojo, ReWAM leads the compared methods without embodied pre-training, with an average score of 9.42 9.42 and a success rate of 5.82 % 5.82\% ( sec. 3.4 ). Embodied pre-training raises these results to 12.29 12.29 and 8.28 % 8.28\% , highlighting ReWAM’s potential to improve further with larger-scale embodied training data. In this setting, ReWAM achieves the highest Generalization score and success rate and the highest Long-Horizon success rate. The benefits of embodied pre-training vary across capabilities. Generalization and Long-Horizon success rates rise from 4.33 % 4.33\% to 10.50 % 10.50\% and from 11.00 % 11.00\% to 16.25 % 16.25\% , respectively. ReWAM remains competitive on Precision tasks without explicit geometric enhancements, though it trails geometry-enhanced methods such as X-VLA Zheng et al. (2025a) and Spatial Forcing Li et al. (2025a) . ReWAM also falls substantially behind the leading methods in Open instruction following. We attribute the gap in open instruction following to the absence of generative video pre-training, which limits instruction generalization.

sections.heading: Reconstruction Fidelity versus Control Utility.
sections.text: We compare Video-VAE and DINO WAMs in tab. 6 . Removing generative video pre-training reduces Fast-WAM’s success by 21.68 / 24.11 21.68/24.11 percentage points on clean/random. Without this pre-training, raw DINO features outperform Video-VAE latents by 4.90 / 9.22 4.90/9.22 points, despite lower RGB reconstruction SSIM ( 0.70 0.70 versus 0.91 0.91 ). An RGB reconstruction codec likewise yields lower success than a DINO reconstruction codec ( tab. 6 ). Reconstruction fidelity thus does not necessarily ensure a representation’s utility for control.

sections.heading: Feature Calibration.
sections.text: Progressively calibrating DINO features with normalization, a representation-aware noise schedule, and multi-layer aggregation yields successive gains of 3.92 3.92 , 1.41 1.41 , and 6.87 6.87 percentage points in average success, as detailed in tab. 6 . Together, these components improve average success by 12.20 12.20 points over raw DINO features. The gains indicate that pre-trained perceptual features benefit from calibration to the distribution and structure required by diffusion-based dynamics modeling.

sections.heading: Temporal Representation Bottleneck.
sections.text: To assess temporal organization, we compare the representation designs in tab. 6 . Fixed random projection concatenates features at each spatial location across a temporal window and projects them to 512 512 dimensions. This simple construction improves average success by 2.89 2.89 percentage points over the calibrated frame-wise baseline, highlighting the value of temporal organization. The result is consistent with prior work on fixed random projections of pre-trained DINO features as prediction latents ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . We also pre-train the TRB as a codec to reconstruct RGB images or DINO features and freeze it during WAM training. The RGB reconstruction codec substantially reduces success, whereas the DINO reconstruction codec falls slightly below fixed random projection on average, suggesting that reconstruction-based training alone is insufficient to improve these temporal representations for control.

sections.heading: Action-Grounded Representation Shaping.
sections.text: AGRS achieves 90.70 % / 89.12 % 90.70\%/89.12\% success on clean/random, outperforming fixed random projection by 3.94 / 3.18 3.94/3.18 percentage points in tab. 6 . The gradient-routing ablation in tab. 6 supports keeping world-loss gradients out of the TRB: allowing them through the current-representation path reduces average success by 6.30 6.30 percentage points, and allowing them through both current and future paths degrades performance further. These results suggest that letting the world objective reshape its prediction targets may encourage representation collapse or predictive shortcuts. The dimensionality comparison in tab. 6 highlights a further advantage of AGRS. Reducing fixed random projection from 512 512 to 128 128 dimensions lowers average success by 3.29 3.29 percentage points. AGRS performs best among the tested widths at 128 128 dimensions and remains effective at 64 64 dimensions. This contrast suggests that action grounding learns more effective control representations, enabling strong performance even at substantially lower dimensionality. sections.heading: \calmregular Action-Related Structure in Representations
sections.text: We investigate the action-related structure in ReWAM and Video-VAE representations using t-SNE and nearest-neighbor direction agreement. Fig. 3 (a) shows independent t-SNE projections of commanded end-effector trajectories and representation variations for the same transitions: one from each of 242 left-arm episodes per task, selected from demonstrations in the random setting. Colors indicate the dominant direction of commanded displacement along the robot’s coordinate axes. Highlighted subsets are balanced across directions by displacement magnitude, while the remaining transitions appear in gray. AGRS exhibits clearer local grouping by direction, suggesting that its representation variations capture action-related information. We also measure whether nearby representation variations correspond to the same motion direction in the original representation space. We find each highlighted transition’s ten nearest neighbors within the balanced subset, excluding itself, and compute the fraction sharing its commanded-motion direction. Fig. 3 (b) reports the mean agreement, which is higher in AGRS space than in Video-VAE space.

sections.heading: \calmregular Real-Robot Evaluation
sections.text: We assess ReWAM on physical hardware across three tasks. Collect Objects requires picking up tabletop items and placing them in a basket; Fold Clothes involves manipulating a garment; and Unpack Lunchbox requires opening a lunchbox and retrieving food. Both methods complete all 20 Collect Objects trials, while ReWAM improves success by 15 percentage points on Fold Clothes and 20 points on Unpack Lunchbox ( fig. 3 ). Across the three tasks, ReWAM succeeds in 55 of 60 trials (91.7%), compared with 48 of 60 (80.0%) for Fast-WAM. These gains highlight ReWAM’s performance advantage on more challenging tasks involving deformable objects and multi-stage manipulation. We also observe autonomous retries, despite their absence from the task demonstrations. Additional real-robot demonstrations are available in the supplementary materials.

sections.heading: \calmregular Conclusion
sections.text: Our study shows that effective world-action modeling depends on how its representation space is constructed and adapted. Reconstruction fidelity alone does not determine control performance, and pre-trained perceptual features benefit from calibration and temporal organization. ReWAM combines these components with action-grounded representation shaping, letting the policy determine what the representation encodes, while the world model learns its dynamics. Results on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, and real-robot manipulation demonstrate the effectiveness of this design without generative video pre-training. These findings highlight the potential of representation design to advance joint prediction and control.

sections.heading: Temporal sampling and horizons.
sections.text: Each training clip contains ten multi-view observations sampled every 8 8 control steps, at offsets [ − 8 , 0 , 8 , 16 , 24 , 32 , 40 , 48 , 56 , 64 ] [-8,0,8,16,24,32,40,48,56,64] . The first pair defines z 0 z_{0} , and the remaining four pairs define z 1 : 4 z_{1:4} over the 64 64 -action horizon. Inference requires only the historical and current observations. At the first query, the current observation substitutes for the missing history. We apply the same substitution during RoboTwin training with probability 0.1 0.1 . Padded targets are excluded from the corresponding losses.

sections.heading: TRB architecture.
sections.text: The head camera yields a 16 × 20 16\times 20 DINO patch grid, and each wrist camera yields an 8 × 10 8\times 10 grid. Spatiotemporal patchification produces 80 + 20 + 20 = 120 80+20+20=120 tokens per state, each initially 8192 8192 -dimensional. A single eight-head attention layer mixes tokens across views within each temporal pair. It uses two-dimensional RoPE with base 10,000 10{,}000 , coordinates scaled by 16 16 , and learned camera-specific query and key biases.

sections.heading: Inference and action execution.
sections.text: At each query, we cache the world branch’s current-state keys and values, generate actions from Gaussian noise using Euler updates with decreasing flow time, and execute a prefix of the predicted chunk. sections.text: The SSIM probe measures how much pixel information can be recovered from the representation. During training, an auxiliary decoder D ψ ​ ( z ¯ j ) D_{\psi}(\bar{z}_{j}) reconstructs future RGB observation pairs from detached latents. The reconstruction loss updates only the decoder parameters ψ \psi , without affecting the encoder or WAM. The decoder is not used at inference.

sections.heading: Data source and transition selection.
sections.text: We examine all 500 500 RoboTwin demonstrations from the random setting for each displayed task. We retain episodes in which the left gripper’s command range exceeds 0.1 0.1 and the right gripper’s does not. Candidate transitions start at 16 , 24 , 32 , … 16,24,32,\ldots and span 32 32 control steps. Throughout each window, including both endpoints, the active gripper’s command and recorded state must remain below 0.2 0.2 and 0.25 0.25 , respectively, in dataset units. We select the middle eligible start in each episode, using the later of the two middle starts when the count is even. This yields 242 242 transitions each for Move Stapler Pad and Place Mouse Pad. Selection uses only action and state records, independently of representation features or projections.

sections.heading: Direction balancing.
sections.text: We assign each transition to the signed axis with the largest absolute endpoint displacement. To qualify for highlighting, a transition must have a displacement of at least 0.04 0.04 m within 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} of that axis. Directions with fewer than 20 20 eligible candidates are excluded. We omit any bin with fewer than three candidates in a retained direction. Both subsets cover + X +X , − X -X , + Y +Y , and − Y -Y .

sections.text: Each t-SNE fit includes all 242 242 transitions, with those outside the highlighted subset shown in gray. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.38163v1 [cs.CV] 29 Sep 2026 \code https://github.com/hustvl/ReWAM Rethinking Representations for World-Action Modeling Haoyi Jiang Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science & Technology Intern at D-Robotics Liu Liu Affiliation: Horizon Robotics Project leader Xinjiang Wang Affiliation: Horizon Robotics Zhihao Sun Affiliation: Fudan University Zequn Chen Affiliation: Horizon Robotics Sen Wang Affiliation: Xi’an Jiaotong University Xinjie Wang Affiliation: Horizon Robotics Xia Chen Affiliation: Horizon Robotics Jingfeng Yao Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science & Technology Weiheng Zhao Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science & Technology Shanglin Yuan Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science & Technology Zhizhong Su Affiliation: Horizon Robotics Wei Sui Affiliation: D-Robotics Wenyu Liu Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science & Technology Xinggang Wang Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science & Technology Corresponding author Abstract World-action models jointly learn robot policies and predict future observations, making the representation space an interface between control and prediction. We study the design of this space through controlled comparisons, finding that neither reconstruction fidelity nor pre-trained perceptual features alone ensure effective policy learning. These findings motivate ReWAM, a representation-centric world-action model built on pre-trained DINO features. Feature Calibration and a Temporal Representation Bottleneck organize these features into compact world states suited to dynamics modeling. Action-Grounded Representation Shaping routes only action-loss gradients to the bottleneck, thereby letting the policy shape what the representation encodes while the world model learns how it evolves. Without generative video pre-training, ReWAM achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0. On RoboDojo, it achieves an average score of 12.29 and a success rate of 8.28% using approximately 600 hours of embodied pre-training data. † † Contact: Haoyi Jiang at haoyi_jiang@hust.edu.cn † † correspondence: Xinggang Wang at xgwang@hust.edu.cn \calmregular Introduction World-action models (WAMs) jointly learn robot policies and predict how the world evolves. Many recent WAMs ( Bi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Ye et al., 2026c ; Yuan et al., 2026b ) build on pre-trained video generators and predict future observations in the latent space of a video variational autoencoder (Video-VAE). These models inherit dynamics priors from large-scale generative video pre-training, but their latent spaces are typically optimized for visual reconstruction. Such spaces may preserve fine-grained appearance details without explicitly prioritizing information relevant to control. The role of world prediction extends beyond producing explicit visual rollouts. Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) retains video co-training while removing future-video denoising at deployment, suggesting that prediction can benefit policies through joint training. This raises a fundamental question: How should the representation space for world-action modeling be defined? Representation-space WAMs use pre-trained perceptual features or learned visual-action tokenizers ( Lyu et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Comparative studies show that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to assess control utility ( Nilaksh et al., 2026 ; Yeom et al., 2026 ) . Our experiments support this distinction: without generative video pre-training, raw DINO features outperform Video-VAE latents on RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , despite lower pixel-reconstruction SSIM. Reconstruction-oriented latents therefore do not by themselves establish effective representations for policy learning. Perceptual features are also not necessarily well suited to dynamics modeling: frame-wise features do not explicitly encode temporal variation, and their statistics may be poorly matched to diffusion training. Calibrating DINO features through multi-layer aggregation, normalization, and a representation-aware diffusion noise schedule improves average success on RoboTwin 2.0 by 12.20 12.20 percentage points. Representation design thus extends beyond the choice of encoder. It must also address how features are prepared for prediction, organized over time, and adapted to the needs of control. We propose a division of roles: the policy shapes what the representation encodes, while the world model learns how that representation evolves. We introduce ReWAM , a representation-centric WAM that implements this principle through Action-Grounded Representation Shaping (AGRS). Feature Calibration prepares frozen DINO features for diffusion modeling, and a Temporal Representation Bottleneck (TRB) organizes them into compact world states. During joint training, AGRS routes only action-loss gradients to the bottleneck, adapting the representation to action prediction. The world model learns how this representation evolves without updating it through its own prediction loss. Fig. 1 provides an overview of ReWAM. Figure 1 : Overview of representations for world-action modeling. Top-left: Video-VAE latents are optimized for visual reconstruction. Top-right: Frozen DINO features inherit priors from perceptual pre-training. Bottom: ReWAM uses a Temporal Representation Bottleneck (TRB) to form compact world states from calibrated DINO features. Action-Grounded Representation Shaping (AGRS) trains the TRB through asymmetric routing of action-loss gradients, while the world model learns state transitions. Without generative video pre-training, ReWAM achieves 93.6% success in both the clean and random settings of RoboTwin 2.0 and leads the compared methods without embodied pre-training on RoboDojo ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . Embodied pre-training further improves its RoboDojo average score to 12.29 and success rate to 8.28%. Together with real-robot evaluations, these findings highlight a promising path for world-action modeling based on pre-trained perceptual priors and representations shaped by the demands of control, without relying on generative video pre-training. Our contributions are threefold: • We show through controlled comparisons that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient for choosing WAM representations, and that perceptual features benefit from calibration for dynamics modeling. • We introduce ReWAM, which lets the action objective shape a compact representation space for joint prediction and control. • We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design without generative video pre-training across two simulation benchmarks and real-robot tasks. \calmregular Related Work \calmregular World-Action Models Unified video and action models couple dynamics prediction with policy learning ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ) . Recent systems build on video generation through joint denoising ( Ye et al., 2026c ) or interactions between world and action streams ( Bi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Motubrain Team et al., 2026 ) . RxBrain ( Liang et al., 2026 ) and Cosmos 3 ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) extend this framework to broader multimodal understanding and generation. Other approaches expose intermediate generative features to the policy ( Pai et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) . Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) removes future-video denoising at deployment, while Faster-WAM ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) studies sparse interactions between video and action prediction under distribution shift. These studies motivate examining how the shared representation interface supports policy learning. Complementary work enriches visual prediction with geometric, motion, and semantic supervision ( Guo et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026c ; Yuan et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026a ) , or aligns policy features with future visual representations ( Zheng et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) . Representation-space approaches use pre-trained visual features for prediction and control. LDA-1B ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) and DexWorldModel ( Deng et al., 2026 ) directly predict DINO features, while VLA-JEPA ( Sun et al., 2026 ) and Being-H0.7 ( Luo et al., 2026 ) use future observations to supervise latent representations that guide action generation. LaWAM ( Chen et al., 2026a ) predicts latent visual subgoals, and GAM ( Han et al., 2026 ) uses geometric foundation features for prediction and action decoding. Learned visual-action tokenizers adapt the interface between perception and control ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , while residual latent actions model changes in DINO features ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) . ReWAM builds on this line of work by calibrating and temporally organizing pre-trained features, then using asymmetric gradient routing to adapt the prediction space to the policy objective during joint world-action training. \calmregular Representations for Prediction and Generation Predictive learning in visual feature spaces supports representation learning and world modeling, as explored by V-JEPA models ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) , DINO-world ( Baldassarre et al., 2025 ) , and Spa3R ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Representation design also matters for generation. REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ) and VA-VAE ( Yao et al., 2025 ) align denoiser features and autoencoder latents, respectively, with pre-trained representations. The representation autoencoder (RAE) ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026 ) uses pre-trained encoders to define generative latent spaces, with subsequent work extending this approach to video generation ( Xie et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026b ) and interactive world modeling ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Probing studies and comparative analyses examine what representations encode and how they support spatial understanding, dynamics prediction, and control ( Huang et al., 2026b ; Yeom et al., 2026 ; Nilaksh et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026a ) . ReWAM addresses the complementary problem of how to construct and adapt a representation space for joint world prediction and policy learning. \calmregular ReWAM \calmregular Overview ReWAM jointly learns an action policy and a predictor of future visual representations. Given the previous and current sampled multi-view observations o − 1 o_{-1} and o 0 o_{0} , proprioception s 0 s_{0} , and a language instruction ℓ \ell , the policy predicts an action chunk a 1 : H a_{1:H} . Here, H H denotes the shared future time horizon, covered by actions and visual states at their respective sampling rates. With observations indexed at the image-sampling rate, ReWAM encodes non-overlapping pairs as z j = E ϕ ​ ( o j − 1 , o j ) . z_{j}=E_{\phi}(o_{j-1},o_{j}). (1) The encoder E ϕ E_{\phi} combines a frozen DINOv3-L backbone, feature calibration, and a trainable TRB with parameters ϕ \phi . The current state z 0 z_{0} conditions both branches, and z 1 : H z_{1:H} provide the world-prediction targets. Sampling and execution details appear in Appendix A . Following Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) , ReWAM uses a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture with world and action Diffusion Transformer (DiT) branches, denoted by W θ W_{	heta} and A θ A_{	heta} . Both branches receive conditioning embeddings c c of ℓ \ell and s 0 s_{0} . Future-state and action tokens attend to current-state world features, but attention between the two token groups is blocked. The world branch uses causal temporal attention and independently sampled noise levels for future states, while the action branch predicts the entire action chunk at once. The conditional model therefore factorizes as p θ ( z 1 : H , a 1 : H ∣ z 0 , c ) = p θ ( z 1 : H ∣ z 0 , c ) p θ ( a 1 : H ∣ z 0 , c ) , p_{	heta}(z_{1:H},a_{1:H}\mid z_{0},c)=p_{	heta}(z_{1:H}\mid z_{0},c)\,p_{	heta}(a_{1:H}\mid z_{0},c), (2) where θ 	heta denotes the trainable WAM parameters. Both branches are trained with flow matching. \calmregular Experiments \calmregular Setup Implementation Details. ReWAM uses frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) features and UMT5 embeddings of language instructions. The world and action DiT branches each contain 30 layers, with hidden widths of 2048 2048 and 1024 1024 , respectively, and approximately 3.58B parameters in total. Head-camera images are resized to 256 × 320 256	imes 320 pixels and wrist-camera images to 128 × 160 128	imes 160 pixels. Actions and proprioception are represented as 14-dimensional joint-and-gripper vectors and standardized using z-score normalization. We train with AdamW on 32 H20 GPUs, with a batch size of 512 and a peak learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} that decays to 10 − 6 10^{-6} on a cosine schedule. RoboTwin 2.0. We train a multi-task policy on the 50-task RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark ( Chen et al., 2025 ) using 2,500 clean trajectories and 25,000 trajectories from the random setting. The main comparison uses five training epochs, aligned with the baseline protocol. Representation comparisons and ablations, including the Fast-WAM baselines, use a matched one-epoch training budget. We evaluate 100 episodes per task in each of the clean and random settings and average success rates across tasks. RoboDojo. We evaluate on the simulation suite of RoboDojo ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , which covers five capability categories: Generalization, Precision, Long-Horizon, Memory, and Open. The training set contains 3,500 trajectories across 35 tasks. We train ReWAM for 50k steps with and without prior embodied pre-training. We report the benchmark’s partial-progress score and binary success rate, averaging each metric across the five categories and comparing methods within each pre-training setting. Embodied Pre-training. To assess the benefit of embodied pre-training with additional data, we pre-train ReWAM and Fast-WAM for 75k steps on the same 600 hours of self-collected real-robot manipulation demonstrations. The dataset covers a broad range of manipulation tasks, with collection environments and camera settings that differ from those used in our downstream real-robot experiments. Real-Robot Evaluation. We evaluate ReWAM on a bimanual Piper platform across three tasks: Collect Objects, Fold Clothes, and Unpack Lunchbox. After embodied pre-training, ReWAM and Fast-WAM each undergo 10k steps of task-specific post-training on demonstrations collected in the target scene. We report success rates over 20 trials per task. \calmregular Main Results ReWAM achieves 93.6% success in both settings of RoboTwin 2.0 ( sec. 3.4 ), exceeding the strongest compared method by 0.2 0.2 percentage points on clean and 1.4 1.4 points on random. Its performance in the random setting indicates robustness to the benchmark’s scene variations without embodied pre-training. On RoboDojo, ReWAM leads the compared methods without embodied pre-training, with an average score of 9.42 9.42 and a success rate of 5.82 % 5.82\% ( sec. 3.4 ). Embodied pre-training raises these results to 12.29 12.29 and 8.28 % 8.28\% , highlighting ReWAM’s potential to improve further with larger-scale embodied training data. In this setting, ReWAM achieves the highest Generalization score and success rate and the highest Long-Horizon success rate. The benefits of embodied pre-training vary across capabilities. Generalization and Long-Horizon success rates rise from 4.33 % 4.33\% to 10.50 % 10.50\% and from 11.00 % 11.00\% to 16.25 % 16.25\% , respectively. ReWAM remains competitive on Precision tasks without explicit geometric enhancements, though it trails geometry-enhanced methods such as X-VLA Zheng et al. (2025a) and Spatial Forcing Li et al. (2025a) . ReWAM also falls substantially behind the leading methods in Open instruction following. Feature Calibration. Progressively calibrating DINO features with normalization, a representation-aware noise schedule, and multi-layer aggregation yields successive gains of 3.92 3.92 , 1.41 1.41 , and 6.87 6.87 percentage points in average success, as detailed in tab. 6 . Together, these components improve average success by 12.20 12.20 points over raw DINO features. The gains indicate that pre-trained perceptual features benefit from calibration to the distribution and structure required by diffusion-based dynamics modeling. Temporal Representation Bottleneck. To assess temporal organization, we compare the representation designs in tab. 6 . Fixed random projection concatenates features at each spatial location across a temporal window and projects them to 512 512 dimensions. This simple construction improves average success by 2.89 2.89 percentage points over the calibrated frame-wise baseline, highlighting the value of temporal organization. The result is consistent with prior work on fixed random projections of pre-trained DINO features as prediction latents ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . We also pre-train the TRB as a codec to reconstruct RGB images or DINO features and freeze it during WAM training. The RGB reconstruction codec substantially reduces success, whereas the DINO reconstruction codec falls slightly below fixed random projection on average, suggesting that reconstruction-based training alone is insufficient to improve these temporal representations for control. AGRS achieves 90.70 % / 89.12 % 90.70\%/89.12\% success on clean/random, outperforming fixed random projection by 3.94 / 3.18 3.94/3.18 percentage points in tab. 6 . The gradient-routing ablation in tab. 6 supports keeping world-loss gradients out of the TRB: allowing them through the current-representation path reduces average success by 6.30 6.30 percentage points, and allowing them through both current and future paths degrades performance further. These results suggest that letting the world objective reshape its prediction targets may encourage representation collapse or predictive shortcuts. The dimensionality comparison in tab. 6 highlights a further advantage of AGRS. Reducing fixed random projection from 512 512 to 128 128 dimensions lowers average success by 3.29 3.29 percentage points. AGRS performs best among the tested widths at 128 128 dimensions and remains effective at 64 64 dimensions. This contrast suggests that action grounding learns more effective control representations, enabling strong performance even at substantially lower dimensionality. Collect Objects requires picking up tabletop items and placing them in a basket; Fold Clothes involves manipulating a garment; and Unpack Lunchbox requires opening a lunchbox and retrieving food. Both methods complete all 20 Collect Objects trials, while ReWAM improves success by 15 percentage points on Fold Clothes and 20 points on Unpack Lunchbox ( fig. 3 ). These gains highlight ReWAM’s performance advantage on more challenging tasks involving deformable objects and multi-stage manipulation. We also observe autonomous retries, despite their absence from the task demonstrations. Additional real-robot demonstrations are available in the supplementary materials. \calmregular Conclusion Our study shows that effective world-action modeling depends on how its representation space is constructed and adapted. Reconstruction fidelity alone does not determine control performance, and pre-trained perceptual features benefit from calibration and temporal organization. ReWAM combines these components with action-grounded representation shaping, letting the policy determine what the representation encodes, while the world model learns its dynamics. Results on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, and real-robot manipulation demonstrate the effectiveness of this design without generative video pre-training.
